ECB: Spain's Pablo Hernández de Cos chosen to succeed Christine Lagarde, a Frenchwoman and a German also join the leadership

Meeting in Brussels on Thursday 26 November, a majority of euro area countries chose Spain's Pablo Hernández de Cos, head of the Bank for International Settlements, to lead the European Central Bank after Christine Lagarde, who leaves on 7 February 2027 [1][5]. He beat the Dutchman Klaas Knot [1].

A majority of euro area countries backed Pablo Hernández de Cos at the Brussels summit on Thursday 26 November; he won more support than Klaas Knot, former governor of the Dutch central bank [1]. The Netherlands itself eventually rallied behind him [8].

In the same package, two other seats on the ECB's executive board go to France's Laurence Boone and Germany's Markus Brunnermeier [1]. Brunnermeier would become chief economist and Laurence Boone would be in charge of market operations [2].

An economist, Hernández de Cos was governor of the Bank of Spain from 2018 to 2024 and chaired the Basel Committee, which sets rules for banks worldwide, from 2019 to 2024 [4]. He has headed the Bank for International Settlements, the "central banks' bank", since 1 July 2025 [4].
If appointed, he will be the first Spaniard to lead the ECB since its creation in 1998 [2].

Christine Lagarde announced on 29 October that she would leave the ECB on 7 February 2027, about nine months before the end of her term in October 2027, without giving an official reason [5]. This timing lets Emmanuel Macron weigh in on the choice of her successor before the French presidential election, Al Jazeera noted [6].
The appointment is not yet final: the European Council is due to decide in December [3]. The ECB meeting of 17 December will still be chaired by Christine Lagarde [3].
The key point: the person who will set the price of money in the euro area from February is now all but known, and is seen as a figure of continuity [3].

The job matters twice as much right now: euro area inflation reached 4% in October, double the 2% target, and the ECB has already raised rates twice this year [3]. Economists see Hernández de Cos as slightly more of a "dove" (more cautious about raising rates) than Klaas Knot, but above all as a pragmatic centrist who would keep Christine Lagarde's line [3]; Commerzbank, which combed through his speeches, puts him among the doves [3].

Looking ahead, Capital Economics expects just one more quarter-point hike before cuts by the end of 2027, and MUFG expects +0.25 points in March, at the first meeting he would chair [3]. An economist quoted by Euronews warns that a change at the top will not, on its own, change interest rate policy [3].
The choice is also a deal between countries: Spain gets the presidency, France and Germany two key seats on the executive board, after a negotiation run as a package [1][2].

The head of the ECB influences the rate on your future mortgage and the interest on your savings. A president seen as more cautious could slow rate hikes, but 4% inflation in the euro area remains his priority.
